Content:
Consider the parabola [MATH: y=x^2-10+41] and the horizontal line [MATH: y = k] where [MATH: k] is a real parameter. For some values of [MATH: k,] the parabola and line will not intersect, as shown in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/bd15eb183efdb98c8a3f746b112faacf]

Content:
Now, it's easy to see that if we increase [MATH: k,] there will be a single value in which the parabola and line intersect at exactly one point.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1e5c710253a321ffc7354ba95d74116d]

Content:
What is the value of [MATH: k] in this case?

Content:
If the line [MATH: y=k] intersects the parabola [MATH: y=x^2 - 10x + 41,] we must have
[MATH: x^2 - 10x + 41 = k.]

Content:
So, our initial geometric problem can now be reduced to a pure algebraic form. We need to determine the value of [MATH: k] such that the above equation has exactly one real solution.

Content:
Recall that a quadratic equation has exactly one real root if the discriminant is zero:
[MATH: \mathcal{D} = 0]

Content:
First, we rewrite the equation in standard quadratic form:

Content:
[MATH: x^{2} − 10x + 41|= k; x^{2} − 10x + 41 − k|= 0; x^{2} − 10x + (41 − k)|= 0]

Content:
The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following:

Content:
[MATH: a = 1, \qquad
b = -10, \qquad
c = 41-k]

Content:
So, computing the discriminant, we get

Content:
[MATH: D|= b^{2} − 4ac; = (− 10)^{2} − 4(1)(41 − k); = 100 − 164 + 4k; = 4k − 64.]

Content:
To have exactly one real solution, we need [MATH: \mathcal{D} = 0{:}]

Content:
[MATH: 4k − 64|= 0; 4k|= 64; k|= (64)/(4); k|= 16]

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that the line [MATH: y = k] and the parabola [MATH: y = x^2-10x+41] intersect at precisely one point if [MATH: k=16.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The line [MATH: y=k] intersects the parabola [MATH: y=-2x^2 + 20x - 60] where
[MATH: -2x^2 + 20x - 60 = k.]

We need to determine the value of [MATH: k] such that this equation has one real solution.

A quadratic equation has exactly one real root if the discriminant is zero: [MATH: \mathcal{D} = 0.]

First, rewrite the equation in standard quadratic form:

[MATH: − 2x^{2} + 20x − 60|= k; − 2x^{2} + 20x + (− 60 − k)|= 0]

The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following:

[MATH: a = -2, \qquad b = 20, \qquad c = -60 - k]

So, computing the discriminant, we get

[MATH: D|= b^{2} − 4ac; = (20)^{2} − 4(− 2)(− 60 − k); = 400 + 8(− 60 − k); = 400 − 480 − 8k; = − 80 − 8k.]

To have exactly one real solution, we need [MATH: \mathcal{D} = 0{:}]

[MATH: − 80 − 8k|= 0; − 8k|= 80; k|= − (80)/(8); k|= − 10]

Thus, the equation of the line is [MATH: y=-10.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The line [MATH: y=4x - k] intersects the parabola [MATH: y=-5x^2 + 10x - 1] where
[MATH: -5x^2 + 10x - 1 = 4x - k.]

We need to determine the value of [MATH: k] such that this equation has one real solution.

A quadratic equation has exactly one real root if the discriminant is zero: [MATH: \mathcal{D} = 0.]

First, rewrite the equation in standard quadratic form:

[MATH: − 5x^{2} + 10x − 1|= 4x − k; − 5x^{2} + 10x − 1 − 4x + k|= 0; − 5x^{2} + 6x + (k − 1)|= 0]

The coefficients of our quadratic equation are the following:

[MATH: a = -5, \qquad b = 6, \qquad c = k-1]

So, computing the discriminant, we get

[MATH: D|= b^{2} − 4ac; = 6^{2} − 4(− 5)(k − 1); = 36 + 20(k − 1); = 36 + 20k − 20; = 16 + 20k.]

To have exactly one real solution, we need [MATH: \mathcal{D} = 0{:}]

[MATH: 16 + 20k|= 0; 20k|= − 16; k|= − (16)/(20); k|= − (4)/(5)]

Thus, the equation of the line is [MATH: y=4x-\left(-\dfrac{4}{5}\right)=4x+\dfrac{4}{5}.] To find the [MATH: x]-coordinate, we solve the original quadratic equation, as follows:

[MATH: − 5x^{2} + 6x + (− (4)/(5) − 1)|= 0; − 5x^{2} + 6x − (9)/(5)|= 0; − 25x^{2} + 30x − 9|= 0; − (25x^{2} − 30x + 9)|= 0; − (5x − 3)^{2}|= 0; 5x − 3|= 0; x|= (3)/(5)]

Finally, we find the [MATH: y]-coordinate by substituting [MATH: x=\dfrac{3}{5}] into one of the two equations and solving:

[MATH: y|= 4((3)/(5)) + (4)/(5); = (12)/(5) + (4)/(5); = (16)/(5)]

Therefore, the point of intersection is [MATH: \Big(\dfrac{3}{5},\dfrac{16}{5}\Big).]

We need to determine the value of [MATH: k] such that this equation has one real solution.

A quadratic equation has exactly one real root if the discriminant is zero: [MATH: \mathcal{D} = 0.]

First, rewrite the equation in standard quadratic form:

[MATH: − 5x^{2} + 10x − 1|= 4x − k; − 5x^{2} + 10x − 1 − 4x + k|= 0; − 5x^{2} + 6x + (k − 1)|= 0]

[MATH: D|= b^{2} − 4ac; = 6^{2} − 4(− 5)(k − 1); = 36 + 20(k − 1); = 36 + 20k − 20; = 16 + 20k.]

To have exactly one real solution, we need [MATH: \mathcal{D} = 0{:}]

[MATH: 16 + 20k|= 0; 20k|= − 16; k|= − (16)/(20); k|= − (4)/(5)]

[MATH: y=4x-\left(-\dfrac{4}{5}\right)=4x+\dfrac{4}{5}.]
To find the [MATH: x]-coordinate, we solve the original quadratic equation, as follows:

[MATH: − 5x^{2} + 6x + (− (4)/(5) − 1)|= 0; − 5x^{2} + 6x − (9)/(5)|= 0; − 25x^{2} + 30x − 9|= 0; − (25x^{2} − 30x + 9)|= 0; − (5x − 3)^{2}|= 0; 5x − 3|= 0; x|= (3)/(5)]

Finally, we find the [MATH: y]-coordinate by substituting [MATH: x=\dfrac{3}{5}] into one of the two equations and solving:

[MATH: y|= 4((3)/(5)) + (4)/(5); = (12)/(5) + (4)/(5); = (16)/(5)]

Therefore, the point of intersection is
[MATH: \Big(\dfrac{3}{5},\dfrac{16}{5}\Big).]
